docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Arya Padiyar — Team 102: Automatic Pill Dispenser Subsystem: Board B — Cap / Lid Sensing

This block diagram shows how my subsystem, Board B, is laid out and how it connects to the team's hub board

  • Power levels: A 9V unregulated wall adapter enters through a DC barrel jack. An L7805CV linear regulator steps it down to 5V, which powers the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano through VBUS. The Nano's on-board LDO supplies 3.3V to the sensor, comparator and all logic.
  • Sensor: A DRV5055 linear Hall-effect sensor detects a magnet in the bottle cap. Its analog output goes to the ADC on RA0, so I can read the raw field strength, and to an LM393 comparator. The comparator gives a clean open/closed digital signal on RB0.
  • Actuator / output: A red status LED on RC5 shows the lid state locally.
  • Team connections: Board B connects to the hub (J2) through 8-pin ribbon connector J1, following the class standard: pins 1–5 digital, 6–7 analog, 8 GND. I use pins 1, 2, 3 and 5, and pins 4, 6 and 7 are spare.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Arya Padiyar | Team 102 | Board B: Cap / Lid Sensing

Board B detects when the pill bottle cap is opened. A magnet in the cap is sensed by a linear Hall-effect sensor, a comparator turns the sensor output into a clean open/closed signal, and a linear regulator supplies the board from an external wall supply. The microcontroller (PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano) was selected by the course and is not compared here.

docs.title: 1. Hall-Effect Lid Sensor
docs.text:
Subsystem: Board B – Cap / Lid Sensing

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.TI DRV5055A1QLPG linear Hall-effect sensor (TO-92)$0.77/eachDRV5055A1QLPG at Mouser * Analog output gives a continuous field-strength reading on the PIC ADC (RA0), which meets the project's analog signal chain requirement and lets the lid threshold be tuned in firmware Runs from the 3.3 V rail (3.0 V to 3.63 V range), so its output (centered at 1.65 V) can never exceed the PIC's 3.3 V ADC input TO-92 through-hole package is easy to hand-solder and to position next to the cap magnet* Low unit cost and a complete TI datasheet * Output is ratiometric, so noise on the 3.3 V rail shows up directly in the reading and the supply needs local decoupling Sensitivity drops to 60 mV/mT at 3.3 V (vs. 100 mV/mT at 5 V), giving less signal swing for the same magnet distance Needs a comparator or a firmware threshold to turn the analog value into a clean open/closed signal Solution Pros Cons Option 2.Allegro A1324LUA-T linear Hall-effect sensor (TO-92)$2.01/eachA1324LUA-T at Mouser * Accurate ratiometric analog output (5 mV/G) with 17 kHz bandwidth, well suited to measuring cap position Rated for -40 °C to 150 °C, far beyond anything a pill bottle will see Same TO-92 through-hole package style as Option 1, so it is easy to solder * Requires a 4.5 V to 5.5 V supply, so it cannot run from the 3.3 V rail, and its output (up to about 5 V) would need a divider before the PIC's 3.3 V ADC pin Higher supply current (6.9 mA typical, 9 mA max) than Option 1 Costs more than twice as much as Option 1, and Allegro lists the LUA-T as "contact factory for availability," which risks long lead times Solution Pros Cons Option 3.Custom: Littelfuse MDSR-4-12-18 reed switch with pull-up resistor and RC low-pass debounce filter$1.44/eachMDSR-4-12-18 at Mouser * The switch itself draws no supply current; only the pull-up resistor draws current when the switch is closed Simple digital open/closed output that can go straight to a PIC input after the RC debounce filter Contacts are rated 0.5 A / 200 VDC, far above the 3.3 V logic signal they would switch * On/off output only, so it does not meet the project's analog signal chain requirement and cannot detect a partly opened cap or a weak or missing magnet (LID_FAULT) Glass envelope is fragile and can crack if the leads are bent close to the body during assembly Mechanical contacts bounce and wear, so extra debounce parts are needed and lifetime is limited by the number of switching cycles

Choice: Option 1: TI DRV5055A1QLPG linear Hall-effect sensor

Rationale: The DRV5055 is the only option that runs directly from the 3.3 V rail and still gives an analog output. Because its output stays between 0 V and 3.3 V, it connects straight to the PIC's ADC with no level shifting. The A1324 needs a 5 V supply and a divider on its output, costs more than twice as much, and has uncertain availability. The reed switch gives only an on/off signal, so it does not meet the analog front-end requirement. The analog reading also lets firmware flag LID_FAULT when the field is outside the expected open/closed range, for example when the magnet is missing. The TO-92 package is easy to hand-solder.

docs.title: 2. Comparator
docs.text:
Subsystem: Board B – Cap / Lid Sensing

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.TI LM393P dual voltage comparator (PDIP-8)$0.53/eachLM393P at Mouser * Operates from 2 V to 30 V, so it runs from the same 3.3 V rail as the Hall sensor Open-collector output is pulled up to 3.3 V, so the signal into the PIC (RB0) is always at a safe logic level Dual comparator in a PDIP-8 through-hole package that is easy to hand-solder* Low supply current (0.45 mA typical, 1 mA max at 5 V) and made by several manufacturers, so it is easy to source * Input common-mode range only reaches VCC - 1.5 V (about 1.8 V on a 3.3 V supply), so the switching threshold must sit below 1.8 V Needs an external pull-up resistor on the output, plus feedback resistors to add hysteresis Rated for 0 °C to 70 °C only, which is fine indoors but narrower than the other options Solution Pros Cons Option 2.Microchip MCP6541-I/P push-pull comparator (PDIP-8)$0.54/eachMCP6541-I/P at Mouser * Rail-to-rail inputs and output, so the threshold can be anywhere in the sensor's 0 V to 3.3 V output range Push-pull output drives the PIC input directly with no pull-up resistor Very low quiescent current (about 600 nA typical)* PDIP-8 through-hole package that is easy to hand-solder * Single comparator per package, so a second channel would need another IC Supply is limited to 1.6 V to 5.5 V, which gives less flexibility than the LM393 Push-pull output cannot be pulled up to a different logic level or wired together with other outputs Solution Pros Cons Option 3.Custom: Microchip MCP6002-I/P op-amp wired as a Schmitt-trigger comparator (PDIP-8)$0.45/eachMCP6002-I/P at Mouser * Threshold and hysteresis are set by resistors, so they can be tuned to the magnet distance in our cap Rail-to-rail input and output and a 1.8 V to 6 V supply range, so it runs from the 3.3 V rail Same Microchip MCP600x op-amp family used in our resistive sensor lab, so the team already knows the part * Op-amps are not designed to run in saturation; their slow recovery and 0.6 V/µs slew rate give slower, less clean edges than a true comparator Needs more external resistors to design, place, and debug No built-in hysteresis, so a wrong resistor value can make the output chatter when the cap is near the threshold

Choice: Option 1: TI LM393P dual voltage comparator

Rationale: The LM393 meets every Board B requirement once the threshold is kept inside its input range. The DRV5055 outputs 1.65 V with no magnet, and its output drops when a north pole faces the sensor. With the cap magnet mounted north-pole-down, the output moves between about 1.65 V (cap open) and well below that (cap closed). A threshold of about 1 V therefore stays inside the LM393's 0 V to 1.8 V common-mode range. The open-collector output with a pull-up to 3.3 V guarantees a safe logic level on RB0. Several manufacturers make the LM393, which protects the build schedule from stock shortages. The MCP6541 is the backup if the common-mode limit causes problems during testing. The op-amp Schmitt trigger was rejected because it needs more parts and switches more slowly than a dedicated comparator.

docs.title: 3. 5 V Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
Subsystem: Board B – Cap / Lid Sensing (power)

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.STMicroelectronics L7805CV 5 V linear regulator (TO-220)$0.60/eachL7805CV at Mouser * Fixed 5 V output rated up to 1.5 A, far more than Board B needs Built-in current limiting and thermal shutdown protect the board from wiring mistakes during bring-up TO-220 through-hole package is easy to solder; at 100 mA from 9 V it dissipates only 0.4 W, so it needs no heatsink* Linear regulator as the course requires, stable with small input and output capacitors * About 2 V dropout means the input must stay above roughly 7 V, which rules out running long from a 9 V battery Quiescent current of a few milliamps is wasted as heat Only about 56 % efficient from a 9 V input (5 V / 9 V); the rest is lost as heat Solution Pros Cons Option 2.TI LM2940CT-5.0/NOPB 5 V low-dropout regulator (TO-220)$2.04/eachLM2940CT-5.0 at Mouser * Low dropout (0.5 V typical at 1 A) lets it keep regulating from a lower input voltage Reverse-polarity protection (-15 V typical) survives a supply plugged in backwards Over 1 A output in a TO-220 through-hole package * Needs an output capacitor of at least 22 µF with ESR between 0.1 Ω and 1 Ω, or it can oscillate High quiescent current (10 mA typical at a 5 mA load), which is more than the Hall sensor and comparator draw combined More than three times the cost of Option 1 Solution Pros Cons Option 3.Microchip MCP1702-5002E/TO 5 V low-dropout regulator (TO-92)$0.65/eachMCP1702-5002E/TO at Mouser * Extremely low quiescent current (2 µA typical) Low dropout (625 mV typical at 250 mA) Stable with small 1 µF ceramic capacitors and takes up little board space * Rated for only 250 mA output, with little margin if more 5 V loads are added later Maximum input voltage is 13.2 V, so there is little headroom for supply spikes or a higher-voltage adapter TO-92 package cannot shed much heat: (9 V - 5 V) × 250 mA = 1 W, which is far too much for TO-92

Choice: Option 1: STMicroelectronics L7805CV

Rationale: Board B runs from a 9 V wall supply, so the L7805's 2 V dropout and few-milliamp quiescent current don't matter. 9 V leaves 4 V of headroom, twice the dropout. At Board B's low current the TO-220 package runs cool with no heatsink. Built-in current limiting and thermal shutdown protect the board during bring-up. It is also the least expensive option and is widely stocked. The LM2940 costs more than three times as much, has strict output-capacitor ESR limits, and draws more quiescent current, and its low-dropout advantage isn't needed with a 9 V input. The MCP1702 is limited to 250 mA and cannot dissipate the heat of a 4 V drop at higher currents.

docs.title: 4. Power Source
docs.text:
Subsystem: Board B – Cap / Lid Sensing (power)

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Adafruit 9 VDC 1000 mA regulated switching wall adapter$8.95/each9 V 1 A adapter at Adafruit * Regulated 9 V stays above the L7805's roughly 7 V minimum input while keeping regulator heat low 5.5 mm / 2.1 mm center-positive plug mates with the PJ-102AH barrel jack on Board B UL listed with a universal 100–240 VAC input* Gives continuous power to a dispenser that sits on a counter all day * Tied to a wall outlet, so the board does not run during a power outage The most expensive item on Board B Adafruit gives a specification list rather than a full manufacturer datasheet Solution Pros Cons Option 2.Adafruit 12 VDC 1000 mA regulated switching wall adapter$8.95/each12 V 1 A adapter at Adafruit * Same 5.5 mm / 2.1 mm center-positive plug, so it mates with the same barrel jack More input headroom above the regulator's dropout Regulated, UL listed, 1 A output * The L7805 must drop 7 V instead of 4 V, so it makes 75 % more heat for the same load current Listed as out of stock at the time of writing, which risks the build schedule Extra voltage brings no benefit, since nothing on Board B needs more than 5 V Solution Pros Cons Option 3.9 V alkaline battery (Energizer 522) with Adafruit 9 V battery clip and 5.5 mm / 2.1 mm plug$2.95/each (clip) + about $6.10/each (battery, Newark)9 V clip at Adafruit, Energizer 522 datasheet * Portable, with no outlet needed The clip's center-positive barrel plug fits the same PJ-102AH jack, so no board change is needed The clip is inexpensive and covers the battery terminals to prevent shorts * Small capacity (about 600 mAh), and the voltage falls below the L7805's roughly 7 V minimum input long before the battery is empty, so battery life is short Batteries must be bought again and again A dispenser that quietly loses power could miss a dose reminder, which defeats the purpose of the product

Choice: Option 1: Adafruit 9 VDC 1000 mA regulated wall adapter

Rationale: A pill dispenser stays in one place and must run reliably every day, so a wall adapter suits it better than a battery. A 9 V battery would drop below the L7805's minimum input early in its discharge. 9 V is the lowest standard adapter voltage that still clears the regulator's 2 V dropout with margin, so it keeps regulator heat lower than the 12 V adapter would. Its 1 A rating is far above what Board B draws. Its 5.5 mm / 2.1 mm plug mates with the PJ-102AH barrel jack already in the block diagram. It is regulated and UL listed, and it is in stock. The 12 V adapter is not.
